subChunks.title: Bounded Contexts, Aggregates & Ubiquitous Language
subChunks.hookHtml: Domain-Driven Design (DDD) is a way of thinking about software that puts the business problem at the centre. When the codebase speaks the same language as the business, fewer things get lost in translation — bugs, misunderstandings, and hidden complexity decrease dramatically. DDD is not a framework; it is a set of thinking tools for complex domains.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Ubiquitous Language

The shared vocabulary that developers and domain experts use consistently — in code, tests, documentation, and conversation. If the business calls it a 'booking' and the code calls it a 'reservation record', misunderstandings accumulate.

Ubiquitous language: the domain expert says 'a mage casts a spell at a cost of mana' → your code has Mage, castSpell(Spell spell), mana field. The term 'cast' is not 'execute' or 'run'. Precision in naming reduces cognitive translation cost.

Bounded Context

A Bounded Context is a logical boundary within which a domain model is consistent and the ubiquitous language is defined. The same word may mean different things in different contexts.

Example: 'Spell' in the Casting Context has: name, mana cost, damage formula, element. 'Spell' in the Library Context has: name, author, publication date, description. They are different models for the same term — and that is correct. They should not share one 'Spell' class across both contexts.

// Casting Context
package com.academy.casting;
record Spell(String id, String name, int manaCost, DamageFormula formula) {}

// Library Context
package com.academy.library;
record Spell(String id, String name, Mage author, LocalDate published) {}
// Same domain term, different model — intentional

Aggregates

An Aggregate is a cluster of domain objects treated as a single unit for data changes. It has a root entity (the Aggregate Root) that controls all access and invariants within the boundary.

Rules: (1) external objects may only hold references to the Aggregate Root, not internal entities. (2) All changes to the aggregate go through the root. (3) Invariants are enforced at the aggregate root level. (4) An aggregate transaction boundary = one DB transaction.

// Order is the Aggregate Root
class Order { // Aggregate Root
    private List<OrderItem> items;  // internal entity
    private Money total;

    // ALL changes go through root methods — not directly to items
    void addItem(Product p, int qty) {
        if (items.size() >= MAX_ITEMS) throw new DomainException("Order is full");
        items.add(new OrderItem(p, qty));
        total = recalculate();
    }
    // invariant: total is always consistent with items
}

Entities vs Value Objects

Entity: defined by identity — two entities with the same data are still different if they have different IDs. Example: User (even if two users have the same name, they are distinct individuals).

Value Object: defined by its attributes — two value objects with the same data are equal. Immutable. No identity. Example: Money(amount=100, currency=GBP), Address, EmailAddress.

Prefer Value Objects when possible — they simplify reasoning (no side effects, equality by value, shareable).

Anti-Corruption Layer

A translation boundary between two bounded contexts (or an external system) that prevents a poorly-modelled external API from corrupting your domain model. You translate external concepts to your domain's language in the ACL rather than leaking external models into your core domain.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's single 'Spell' model was used for everything: casting, library cataloguing, admin management, tournament scoring. Every field added for one use case cluttered every other use case. Changing the casting logic required understanding library fields. The model grew to 47 fields and 12 optional nulls. Eventually someone drew a bounded context diagram and found there were actually five distinct Spell models that had been collapsed into one catastrophe.

storyBeats.speaker: Domain Architect Phari
storyBeats.text: The fundamental mistake in software is treating domain concepts as data records instead of as models of behaviour. A Spell is not a row in a table with 47 columns. A Spell in the casting context is a rule about mana cost and effect. A Spell in the library context is an intellectual work with an author. Same word, completely different concerns. DDD teaches you to draw those boundaries explicitly.

storyBeats.speaker: Domain Architect Phari
storyBeats.text: The Aggregate Root is the gatekeeper. Nothing inside the aggregate is touched except through its root. This sounds restrictive but it is liberating: if you want to understand what can happen to an Order, you read the Order class. You do not need to search the codebase for places that directly mutate OrderItems. The invariant guarantee is total and localised.

storyBeats.speaker: Value Object for type safety
Domain Architect Phari
storyBeats.text: Ubiquitous language is the hidden dividend of DDD. When every class name, method name, and variable name uses the same terms as the domain expert, onboarding new engineers is faster, conversations about bugs are clearer, and requirements map directly to code. The language gap between code and business is where complexity hides.

learningObjectives: Define ubiquitous language and explain why consistent terminology between code and business reduces complexity
Explain bounded contexts and give an example of the same domain term meaning different things in two contexts
Describe the Aggregate pattern: what the root is, what rules govern access, and why it enforces invariants
Distinguish entities (identity-based equality) from value objects (attribute-based equality, immutable)
commonMistakes: One mega-model for a domain concept used across all bounded contexts — creates a class with too many responsibilities
Allowing external code to directly mutate internal aggregate entities — bypasses invariant enforcement
Using primitive types (String email, String name) instead of Value Objects — allows invalid states and confuses parameter order
Treating DDD as 'just naming things nicely' — the real value is in boundary discovery and invariant enforcement
assessmentCriteria: Can identify at least two distinct bounded contexts in a given system description and name what 'User' or 'Product' means in each
Can write an Aggregate Root with at least one enforced invariant that prevents illegal state
Can refactor a method signature using Value Objects to make illegal argument order a compile-time error
Can explain why two Aggregate instances with the same data may or may not be equal, depending on whether they are Entities or Value Objects
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain DDD bounded contexts to a developer who has one giant 'User' class used everywhere in their monolith. What is a bounded context? Why is having separate User models for different contexts better? What do you lose and gain?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Answer the following DDD design questions:

  1. You are designing an e-commerce system. Identify two bounded contexts and describe what 'Product' means in each (attributes, operations).
  2. Model a ShoppingCart as an Aggregate Root. List the internal entities, the invariant the root must enforce (e.g. max items, non-negative quantities), and explain why cartItem.setQuantity(-1) should not be allowed from outside the aggregate.
  3. Refactor this method signature to use Value Objects: void createAccount(String email, String password, int age, String country). Name three Value Objects and explain what validation each should enforce.
  4. A Mage record contains id, name, school. Two Mage objects have the same name and school but different IDs. Are they the same? Explain using Entity/Value Object terminology.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Two bounded contexts for 'Product':
   
   Catalogue Context (browsing, search):
   Product { id, name, description, images[], price, categoryId, tags[] }
   Operations: search, filter by category, display description
   'Price' here is the display/list price.
   
   Inventory Context (warehouse, stock management):
   Product { sku, warehouseLocation, stockLevel, reorderPoint, supplierId }
   Operations: adjustStock, reserveForOrder, triggerReorder
   'Price' is irrelevant here — inventory cares about physical location and quantity.
   
   Same word 'Product' — two completely different models. They should NOT share a class.

2. ShoppingCart Aggregate:
   Root: ShoppingCart (holds cartId, userId, items, totalPrice)
   Internal entity: CartItem (itemId, productId, quantity, unitPrice)
   
   Invariants the root enforces:
   - Maximum 50 items in a cart
   - No item with quantity < 1
   - totalPrice always equals sum(items.unitPrice × items.quantity)
   
   Why cartItem.setQuantity(-1) should be blocked:
   If external code can directly mutate CartItem, the invariant 'no negative quantity' and 'total stays consistent' cannot be guaranteed. The Cart has no way to know the mutation happened.
   Correct approach: cart.updateItemQuantity(itemId, newQty) — the root validates, updates the item, recalculates total. Invariants remain enforced.

3. Value Objects for createAccount:
   Email: validates format (contains @, valid domain), case-normalises (lowercase)
   HashedPassword: takes raw password, validates length/complexity, stores BCrypt hash; never returns plaintext
   Age: validates range (16–130), represents meaningful domain concept
   Country: validates against ISO 3166 country code list
   
   New signature: void createAccount(Email email, HashedPassword password, Age age, Country country)
   Wrong argument order is now a compile error — you cannot pass a Country where an Email is expected.

4. Two Mage objects with same name/school but different IDs:
   They are NOT the same. Mage is an Entity — identity is defined by the id field.
   Two separate individuals who happen to have the same name are still two distinct people.
   mage1.equals(mage2) → false (based on id comparison).
   If Mage were a Value Object (defined by its attributes), they would be equal. But domain reality says mages are individuals with persistent identity across time — changing a mage's name doesn't change which mage they are. That is the entity distinction.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Design the domain model for the Academy's Tournament bounded context. A Tournament has a schedule of matches; each match involves two competitors and produces a result. Answer:

  1. Identify the Aggregate Root and all internal entities
  2. List at least three invariants the root must enforce
  3. Identify any Value Objects in the model and explain why they are Value Objects
  4. There is also an existing Registration context where 'Tournament' means something different (a registration event with a date, entry fee, and eligibility criteria). Describe what 'Tournament' looks like in each context — and why they should be separate models
subChunks.modelAnswer:
1. Tournament domain model:
   Aggregate Root: Tournament (holds id, name, status, List<Match> matches)
   Internal entities: Match (matchId, competitor1Id, competitor2Id, scheduledTime, MatchResult)
   MatchResult is a Value Object (defined by values: winner, score, completedAt)

2. Invariants the Tournament root enforces:
   - Cannot schedule a match if Tournament status is COMPLETED or CANCELLED
   - Cannot have the same competitor in two simultaneous matches (time overlap check)
   - Cannot record a result for a match that has already been decided
   - Cannot add matches after the Tournament has started (status = IN_PROGRESS)
   - Match count cannot exceed the maximum capacity defined at creation

3. Value Objects:
   MatchResult(winnerId, score, completedAt) — a completed result is defined entirely by these attributes.
     Two MatchResults with the same winner, score, and time are the same result (no individual identity needed).
   Score(mageAPoints, mageBPoints) — purely attribute-defined, immutable.

4. Tournament in two bounded contexts:

   Tournament Context (match scheduling, results):
   Tournament { id, name, status(SCHEDULED/IN_PROGRESS/COMPLETED), List<Match> matches }
   Concern: match execution, results recording, competitor advancement
   'Competitor' here is a lightweight reference (just the competing mage ID and bracket position)

   Registration Context (sign-up, eligibility, fees):
   Tournament { id, name, startDate, entryFee, eligibleTiers, maxEntrants, registrations[] }
   Concern: who can enter, collecting fees, forming the competitor list
   'Tournament' here cares about date, money, tier rules

   Why separate: registering for a tournament (can I enter? what does it cost?) is a completely different workflow from running a tournament (who fights whom? who won?). Merging them creates a class that must change for both registration rule changes AND match scheduling changes — high coupling, low cohesion. An Anti-Corruption Layer translates the registered competitor list from the Registration context into Match entities in the Tournament context when the tournament starts.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a Bounded Context in Domain-Driven Design?
options: To limit the size of a Java class
To define a boundary within which a domain model is consistent and the ubiquitous language has a specific meaning
To restrict which teams can modify a service
To enforce transaction boundaries in the database
questions.answer: To define a boundary within which a domain model is consistent and the ubiquitous language has a specific meaning
questions.explanation: A Bounded Context is an explicit boundary within which domain concepts have consistent definitions. The same word ('Order', 'Customer', 'Spell') may mean something different in different contexts — a Bounded Context makes that distinction explicit and prevents the accidental merging of incompatible models. It also corresponds to a team ownership boundary and often a service/module boundary.

questions.prompt: An Order aggregate has internal OrderItems. External code directly calls orderItem.setStatus(CANCELLED). What DDD rule does this violate?
options: Ubiquitous language — 'setStatus' is not a domain term
Value Object immutability — OrderItem must be a Value Object
Aggregate boundary — changes to internals must go through the Aggregate Root
Bounded Context — status changes belong in a different context
questions.answer: Aggregate boundary — changes to internals must go through the Aggregate Root
questions.explanation: The Aggregate rule is that all state changes to entities within an aggregate must go through the Aggregate Root. Direct mutation of internal entities (OrderItem) bypasses the root's invariant enforcement — the Order cannot ensure its own consistency (e.g. recalculating total, checking cancellation eligibility) if external code mutates its items directly. Correct pattern: order.cancelItem(itemId) — the root validates and executes the change.

questions.prompt: You have a Money class with amount and currency. Two instances with amount=100, currency=GBP are created independently. Should money1.equals(money2) return true? What DDD concept determines this?
options: Yes — Money is a Value Object; equality is defined by attribute values, not identity
No — Money is an Entity; it has a unique ID
It depends on whether the Money was created in the same transaction
No — mutable objects should never be considered equal
questions.answer: Yes — Money is a Value Object; equality is defined by attribute values, not identity
questions.explanation: Money(100, GBP) is a classic Value Object. There is no meaningful distinction between two separate instances both representing £100 — they are conceptually the same value. Value Objects are defined by their attributes, are immutable, and use value-based equality (equals/hashCode based on all fields). Unlike an Entity (e.g. a specific bank account), a Money amount has no individual identity — £100 is £100 regardless of which Money object represents it.
